chapters.title: Chapter 7: Extreme Value Theory for Tail Risk

lessons.title: Estimating Tail Risk with EVT: The Hill Estimator

children.text: The last lesson estimated the GPD shape parameter using the method of moments, fitting both a shape and a scale parameter to the exceedance data. The Hill estimator, proposed by Bruce Hill in 1975 and still one of the most widely used tools in extreme value statistics, takes a narrower, more direct approach: estimate the tail index alone, using nothing but the log-ratios of the largest observations, with no threshold subtraction and no scale parameter to fit.

body.label: Hill Estimator
body.value: A tail index estimate built purely from the log-ratios of the top k largest observations in a sample
body.context: Applies specifically to power-law, fat-tailed data, the xi greater than 0 case from the last lesson.

body.caption: X_(1) is the largest observation in the sample, X_(2) the second largest, and so on. X_(k+1) is the (k+1)-th largest, acting as an implicit threshold. This estimates the same shape parameter, xi, used in the GPD from the last lesson.

children.text: Applying Hill to the Same Data

Converting the last lesson's 25 exceedances back into actual daily losses, by adding the 2.0% threshold back to each, gives the top 25 losses out of the original 250-day sample, sorted from largest to smallest: 4.10%, 3.50%, 3.20%, 3.00%, 2.85%, and so on down to 2.05%. The Hill estimator can be applied using any choice of k, the number of top observations included.

body.caption: Hill estimator applied at different values of k

body.text: The Hill estimate drifts modestly as k changes, from about 0.20 at k=5 down to about 0.18 at k=20, a roughly 13% relative change. That is a reasonably stable range for a small sample like this one, but it is not a coincidence that the estimate moves at all, this sensitivity to k is one of the Hill estimator's best-known practical limitations, sometimes visualized as a 'Hill plot', graphing the estimate against k and looking for a stable plateau rather than trusting any single value.

children.text: Why Hill and GPD Method-of-Moments Disagree

Here is the uncomfortable part. The Hill estimates above, roughly 0.18 to 0.20, are noticeably higher than the last lesson's GPD method-of-moments estimate for essentially the same data, xi = 0.0355. Both methods are asymptotically valid estimators of the same underlying parameter, but they behave differently in a small, finite sample like this 25-observation tail. Method of moments uses the exceedances' mean and variance jointly to solve for both shape and scale at once. Hill uses only log-ratios of the raw order statistics and estimates shape alone, more directly, but with its own sensitivity to exactly how many top observations, k, are included.

columns.label: GPD Method-of-Moments
points: Estimates shape and scale together from exceedance mean and variance
Applies to any xi, positive, zero, or negative
Requires an explicit threshold to define the exceedances first

columns.label: Hill Estimator
points: Estimates shape alone, from log-ratios of top-k order statistics
Only valid for the xi greater than 0, genuinely fat-tailed case
The implicit threshold is just whichever k you choose, easy to vary and re-check

body.text: This is not a sign that either estimator is broken. It is a genuine, well-documented feature of small-sample tail estimation: different valid methods, applied to the same limited extreme data, can produce meaningfully different point estimates. The correct response is the same one Chapter 3 recommended when two VaR models disagreed, treat the disagreement as diagnostic information rather than picking whichever number is more convenient. A serious tail-risk estimate should be checked across more than one method and more than one threshold or k choice, and reported with that uncertainty made visible, not hidden behind a single precise-looking decimal.

body.title: Compute a Hill Estimate by Hand
body.prompt: Using k=3 top observations, X(1)=10, X(2)=8, X(3)=7, and X(4)=6 as the (k+1)-th value, compute the Hill estimator: gamma-hat = (1/k) x [ln(X(1)/X(4)) + ln(X(2)/X(4)) + ln(X(3)/X(4))].
body.explanation: ln(10/6) = 0.5108, ln(8/6) = 0.2877, ln(7/6) = 0.1542. Summing gives 0.9527, divided by k=3 gives approximately 0.3176.

body.title: Reconciling Two Disagreeing Tail Estimates
body.scenario: A risk analyst reports a GPD-based extreme VaR figure to the risk committee using xi = 0.0355 from the method-of-moments fit. A colleague, using the Hill estimator on the same underlying data, arrives at xi around 0.19, nearly 5 times larger, and a correspondingly much higher extreme VaR estimate.
body.prompt: How should the analyst present this disagreement to the risk committee, rather than simply picking one number to report?
body.modelAnswer: The analyst should present both estimates and the range of extreme VaR figures they imply, rather than silently choosing one, since the gap itself is meaningful information about how much genuine uncertainty exists in this particular tail estimate. Useful next steps include checking Hill's stability across a range of k values, as this lesson did, checking the GPD fit's stability across different threshold choices, as the last lesson discussed, and considering whether the sample simply has too few extreme observations for either method to be trusted with high precision. Reporting a range, or the more conservative of the two figures with a clear caveat, is more honest and more useful to a risk committee than reporting one precise-looking number that hides real underlying uncertainty.

body.text: Two honest, correctly applied tail estimation methods can disagree meaningfully on the same data. That disagreement is not noise to be resolved by picking a favorite number, it is the clearest signal available of how much genuine uncertainty sits inside a deep-tail risk estimate.

points: The Hill estimator estimates the tail index directly from the log-ratios of the top k largest observations, without needing an explicit threshold subtraction or a separately fitted scale parameter, but it only applies to the genuinely fat-tailed, xi greater than 0, case.

The Hill estimate showed mild but real sensitivity to the choice of k, drifting from about 0.20 to about 0.18 as k rose from 5 to 20 in the worked example, a known limitation often checked with a Hill plot.

On the same underlying data, the Hill estimator and the GPD method-of-moments estimator from the last lesson produced meaningfully different tail index estimates, 0.18 to 0.20 versus 0.0355, a genuine, well-documented feature of small-sample tail estimation rather than an error in either method.

When tail estimation methods disagree, the right response is to report the disagreement and investigate its source, exactly as Chapter 3 recommended for disagreeing VaR models, rather than silently picking whichever estimate is more convenient.

The next and final lesson of this chapter brings GPD and Hill together into a complete EVT-based VaR and Expected Shortfall framework, addressing directly how to handle exactly this kind of estimator disagreement in practice.
